name: go-quickjs
baseline: QuickJS (C, release 2026-06-04) and goja (pure-Go JavaScript engine)
workload: Mozilla AreWeFastYet V8 version 7 suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) as median of three fresh-process runs, plus QuickJS's own tests/microbench.js.
claimed_speedup: Versus goja (Apple M5 Max, Go 1.27.0): V8 v7 composite score 3,748 vs 720 (5.21x), wall time 22.51 s vs 53.37 s, 60.2% less allocation. Versus C QuickJS 2026-06-04 (AMD Ryzen 5 3600, Windows, Go 1.27.1): composite score 1,454 vs 1,315 (about 11% higher) and fixed-run total 1,690 ms vs 2,589 ms (0.65x QuickJS's time). Micro-benchmarks go the other way: 1.15x QuickJS's time by geometric mean over 71 tests.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.0 (goja comparison, go-quickjs commit 04bbeec) and Go 1.27.1 (QuickJS comparison, go-quickjs 4629679 / v0.21.1); go build flags not stated; build flags of the C QuickJS binary not stated.
hardware: Apple M5 Max (macOS ARM64) for the goja comparison; AMD Ryzen 5 3600 (Windows) for the C QuickJS comparison.
tradeoffs: Pure Go reimplementation of QuickJS-NG with no cgo, WebAssembly or C toolchain, so it cross-compiles anywhere Go does; ships an embeddable engine, a qjs-style CLI and ECMAScript regex support. README reports 99,595 of 99,937 test262 variants passing (342 skipped). Go's switch dispatch costs about twice QuickJS per instruction, partly offset by running hot functions as trees of Go closures; Go GC instead of QuickJS reference counting; Intl through go-intl.
caveats: First-party numbers from a very young project (3 stars). The suite-level win over C QuickJS comes mostly from RegExp (0.30x of QuickJS's time) and Splay allocation setup; single operations are slower (slower on 48 of 71 micro-benchmarks, up to 3.5x on weak_map_set), and the author notes the fixed-run and scored-run margins disagree (0.65x time vs 11% score) because they time different things. The two comparisons ran on different machines and operating systems. Baseline goja is another pure-Go engine, not the category incumbent V8. LICENSE file carries Fabrice Bellard's copyright (derived from QuickJS-NG). Numbers were read from the repo docs; the discovering page was the go-js-engines-benchmark shootout (by the author of a competing engine, QJS) in a search snippet.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch '"faster than QuickJS" JavaScript engine interpreter blog post 2026 benchmark' returned the go-quickjs/go-js-engines-benchmark page (dated 2026-10-05); opened that repo, then the go-quickjs repo and docs/benchmarks.md.

name: Paserati
baseline: goja (pure-Go JavaScript engine) and 'QJS' (QuickJS runner binary; README does not say whether it is native C QuickJS or the fastschema/qjs Wasm build)
workload: bench/bench.js (arithmetic and array microbenchmark) and bench/objects.js (object-heavy microbenchmark) timed with hyperfine via bench/hyperfine.sh.
claimed_speedup: bench/bench.js: Paserati 3.924 s vs goja 5.207 s (1.33x faster) vs QJS 4.945 s (1.26x faster); bench/objects.js: 6.169 s vs goja 7.015 s (1.14x) vs QJS 8.135 s (1.32x).
tradeoffs: Experimental TypeScript runtime: parses and type-checks TypeScript, compiles directly to bytecode for a register VM with inline caches and shape-based objects, no JIT. README reports Test262 language 98.3% and built-ins 89.9%. The third-party go-js-engines-benchmark runs it with type checking disabled.
caveats: First-party, two simple microbenchmarks, no hardware, compiler or Go version stated; README itself says it has a long way to go performance-wise. Identity of 'QJS' is ambiguous. In the go-quickjs/go-js-engines-benchmark shootout (Apple M5 Max, Go 1.27.0, type checking disabled, written by the author of competing engine QJS) Paserati scores 1,125 on the V8 v7 suite vs goja 751, but far below GoQuickJS at 3,912. V8-suite results referenced by the README live on a blocked github.io page.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch '"faster than QuickJS" JavaScript engine interpreter blog post 2026 benchmark' led to the go-js-engines-benchmark page, which lists Paserati; opened the Paserati repo and README.

name: luars (lua-rs)
workload: Fourteen Lua benchmark scripts (bench_arithmetic.lua through bench_errors.lua) run by run_benchmarks.ps1; value is luars throughput divided by native Lua throughput times 100.
claimed_speedup: Windows snapshot, Ryzen 7 5800X: arithmetic 111%, locals 132%, table library 118%, coroutines 152%, errors 103% of native Lua 5.5; but control flow 87%, functions 92%, closures 80%, multiple returns 78%, tables 92%, iterators 93%, math 98%, metatables 78%, OOP 92% (9 of 14 scripts below parity). README says Linux runs are often 20% to 40% slower than native Lua while still winning a subset, and that macOS generally outperforms native Lua (no numbers).
tradeoffs: Pure Rust Lua 5.5 runtime with embedding toolkit, derive macros, standalone interpreter, debugger integration and a WASM target; unsafe code concentrated in GC representation, stack handling and hot VM paths; README says it passes the official Lua test suite with expected skips.
caveats: Mixed result, not faster overall: most scripts are slower than native Lua and the README itself reports 20-40% slower on Linux, with no maintained Linux snapshot. The author attributes the Windows coroutine win (152%) partly to native Lua's longjmp cost on Windows. Native Lua build, Rust compiler and flags not stated; string benchmarks omitted from the chart. A search snippet of an older README described the project as mostly AI-assisted (snippet only, not verified in the repo).
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'pure Rust OR Zig OR Go Lua 5.4 5.5 VM implementation "faster than" reference C Lua benchmark results README blog' surfaced github.com/CppCXY/lua-rs; numbers read from the repo docs.

name: jrsonnet
baseline: google/jsonnet C++ reference implementation (v0.22.0-rc1); also go-jsonnet v0.22.0-rc1 and Sjsonnet 0.6.2
workload: Jsonnet evaluation wall time: real-world GraalVM CI and kube-prometheus manifests, the C++ jsonnet perf_tests and benchmarks suites, and Go jsonnet builtin benchmarks; mean and sigma tables per implementation.
claimed_speedup: C++ perf_test 'Large string join': jrsonnet 2.6 ms vs C++ 39.7 ms (15.44x) and Go 46.4 ms. C++ 'Tail call' benchmark: 865.2 us vs C++ 18,460.1 us (21.34x) and Go 2,559.0 us (2.96x). GraalVM CI: 34.4 ms vs Go 600.3 ms (17.47x), C++ did not finish within an hour. Kube-prometheus manifests: 43.6 ms vs Go 1,068.4 ms (24.52x), C++ took hours. Ratios as printed in the doc.
compiler_and_flags: Tested versions listed: jrsonnet 0.5.0-pre97, C++ and Go jsonnet v0.22.0-rc1, Sjsonnet 0.6.2, rsjsonnet 2026-03-23; Rust compiler, build profile and flags not stated.
tradeoffs: Rust library and CLI; also ships libjsonnet.so-compatible C/C++ bindings plus Python (rjsonnet), WASM/JavaScript and in-progress Java bindings, so it is callable from C++. Adds experimental syntax extensions beyond standard Jsonnet (features guide). Jsonnet is a data templating language, so this only loosely fits the language-interpreter category.
caveats: Maintainer's own benchmark document: benchmark driver, run counts and build profile are not in the doc, only the source programs, versions and CPU. Many rows are microsecond to few-millisecond scale and probably dominated by process startup. C++ results are omitted for the heaviest workloads because they took hours, and C++ and Go are release-candidate versions. Repository was renamed from CertainLach/jrsonnet; deltarocks/jrsonnet is the canonical URL after redirect.
found_via: Blogs / talks: not named in any blog snippet; found by opening READMEs of niche language-interpreter implementations after the WebSearch snippets ran out. README states 'performance better than all existing implementations' and links docs/benchmarks.adoc.

name: bc and dc (Gavin Howard)
workload: bc scripts run through tests/script.sh (add, subtract, multiply, divide), 1234567890^100000, a patched timeconst.bc script and two 100,000,000-iteration loop scripts; best of four runs, wall-clock seconds.
claimed_speedup: With -O2 and no LTO (wall time, GNU bc vs this bc): addition 2.54 s vs 0.88 s, multiplication 7.15 s vs 2.20 s, division 3.36 s vs 1.61 s, power 11.30 s vs 0.73 s, timeconst.bc 16.71 s vs 13.16 s. With -O3 -flto -march=native: power 11.08 s vs 0.71 s, multiplication 7.01 s vs 1.59 s. Slower on a plain for-loop script (16.60 s GNU vs 22.76 s this bc at -O2).
compiler_and_flags: clang 9.0.1; both bc builds compiled with the same flags: -O2 without LTO, then -O3 -flto -march=native, then -O3 -flto.
hardware: x86_64 machine running Gentoo Linux; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: POSIX bc plus dc in one binary and the bcl C library (callable from C++). Speed comes from packing several decimal digits per hardware integer and Karatsuba multiplication; author says the interpreter loop itself is slightly slower than GNU bc on scripts with little math.
caveats: Numbers are from bc 3.0.0 (2019) against GNU bc 1.07.1 with no CPU model, and the project has had many releases since; best-of-four runs; the win is arithmetic-library speed, not general interpreter throughput (loop scripts are slower or level); first-party measurements. GNU bc is not one of the category baselines and bc is a calculator language rather than a general scripting language.
found_via: Blogs / talks: not named in any blog snippet; found by checking niche language interpreters with published speed comparisons. README states 'This bc is faster' and links manuals/benchmarks.md.

name: Regorus
baseline: OPA (Open Policy Agent, Go) opa eval
workload: Evaluating the Azure Container Instances Rego policy in tests/aci (query data.framework.mount_overlay) with hyperfine on both command-line tools.
claimed_speedup: regorus eval 4.6 ms +/- 0.2 ms vs opa eval 45.2 ms +/- 0.6 ms (about 10x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Rego (OPA policy language) interpreter in Rust; mostly compliant with the OPA v1.2.0 test suite but not all builtins are implemented; no_std capable. Bindings for C, C++ (cbindgen with corrosion-rs CMake integration), C#, Go, Java, JavaScript/WASM, Python and Ruby.
caveats: Whole-process timings of two CLIs: Go runtime startup and policy loading probably account for much of OPA's 45 ms, so the evaluation-speed ratio is unclear. No hardware, OPA version, regorus build profile or run commands for building the binaries are stated. Rego is a policy language, not one of the category's general-purpose baselines.
found_via: Blogs / talks: not named in any blog snippet; opened the README while checking policy and configuration-language interpreters (README 'Performance' section).

name: QJS (fastschema/qjs)
baseline: goja (pure-Go JavaScript engine) and ModerncQuickJS (QuickJS translated to Go with ccgo)
workload: factorial(10) computed 1,000,000 times (five iterations) and the AreWeFastYet V8 version 7 suite.
claimed_speedup: Factorial average 746.132 ms vs goja 1.127 s (1.51x) and ModerncQuickJS 1.910 s (2.56x). V8 v7 score 498 vs goja 442 and ModerncQuickJS 323; suite duration 72.0 s vs 78.3 s and 97.2 s. goja wins the RegExp row (381 vs 142).
tradeoffs: Runs QuickJS compiled to WebAssembly under wazero: no cgo, sandbox isolation and memory limits, ES2023 features through QuickJS; Go and JavaScript values cross a Wasm boundary (ProxyValue exists to avoid copies). Requires Go 1.22 or later.
caveats: Baselines are other Go-embedded JavaScript engines; it is not compared against native C QuickJS, which a Wasm build would not be expected to beat. Go version and build flags not stated, first-party numbers. A competing project's shootout (go-quickjs/go-js-engines-benchmark, Apple M5 Max) shows this engine at 761 vs goja 751 on the same suite, much closer than here. Stars not retrieved.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch '"faster than QuickJS" JavaScript engine interpreter blog post 2026 benchmark' led to the go-js-engines-benchmark page, which lists QJS; opened the fastschema/qjs README.

name: Monty (pydantic/monty)
baseline: CPython-based sandboxes: local Docker, WASI/wasmtime and Pyodide in Deno (per project docs); no CPython execution-speed claim in the repo docs
workload: Time to get a fresh sandbox and run `1 + 1`, and 10 REPL commands against an existing sandbox (project docs latency table).
claimed_speedup: OSS Monty new sandbox 0.80 ms (from a pre-created pool) vs 16 ms WASI/wasmtime, 195 ms local Docker, 2,700 ms Pyodide in Deno; 10-command agent run 0.40 ms vs 180 ms WASI, 700 ms Docker, 35 ms Pyodide; combined 1.20 ms vs 200 ms, 900 ms and 2,700 ms. README: under 1 ms from a running pool vs about 1,500 ms for a sandbox service.
tradeoffs: Minimal Python sandbox interpreter written in Rust for AI-generated code: no filesystem, environment or network unless functions and mounts are passed in; not a drop-in CPython replacement. Python, JavaScript and Rust packages; a commercial server variant (Full Monty) exists.
caveats: The claim is sandbox startup latency against container and Wasm sandboxes, not interpreter throughput against CPython, so it does not meet the category baselines. Footnote in the docs says Monty's number is a checkout from an already-created pool while the others start from nothing. No hardware stated. The repo has a monty-bench crate comparing Monty with CPython locally, but its numbers are not in the repo; a search snippet of project material said runtime speed is generally between 5x faster and 5x slower than CPython (snippet only). Vendor blog and docs site pydantic.dev blocked here.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Monty minimal Python interpreter Rust pydantic startup time vs CPython' (pydantic.dev article and Show HN thread titles); read the repo README, crates/monty-bench and docs/index.md.

claimed_speedup: No numbers readable: the README shows a bar chart image comparing pocketlang (pre-alpha) with Wren v0.3.0, Python 3.7.4 and Ruby 2.7.2 and calls the language 'fast'; chart values could not be read here (image host not reachable).
hardware: Windows 10 (64-bit), ASUS N552VX, Intel Core i7-6700HQ 2.6GHz, 12GB RAM
